Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 200 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018-19) 
 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 200 is  located in east-central Alberta. The unit  is adjacent to the border of 
Saskatchewan and is approximately 2,726 km2. The habitat is dominated by aspen parkland interspersed with  
native grassland and agricultural land. The eastern edge of the Neutral Hills extends into the unit.  
Previous aerial ungulate surveys conducted in these units have used the strip transect survey method and were 
conducted with the most recent survey in 20 09. Previous white -tailed deer, mule deer, and moose estimates 
have ranged from 1798-5982, 1673-6148, and 89-948, respectively. In previous survey  years, population 
estimates were not determined for elk. Elk observed during the survey were recorded, but gi ven the behaviour 
and movement of elk, this type of survey is not appropriate to determine a population estimate.

Survey Method 
From January 28 -30, 2019, a strip transect survey of WMU 200 was conducted flying north-south lines at 1. 6 
kilometre (1 mile) intervals resulting in a 25% coverage (with 400-metre wide survey strip). Snow conditions were 
poor, degrading from the eastern edge of the unit to the western edge . At each observation point, ungulates 
were counted by species, and when possible, classified by sex and age. Bucks were al so classified by a ntler 
size as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside 
ears) or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears).  Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 
2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average density (R; #/km2) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose by 
summing the total animals counted per transect ( ∑x) by total area searched (length of transects multiplied by 
400 m survey strip [ ∑z]). For a popul ation estimate (unequal sized units, sampling without replacement), we 
multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WMU (Z). A correction factor for detectability 
(estimated at 83%; Habib et al. 2012) can be applied to WTDE and MUDE densit y and population estimates in 
the Parkland for strip widths of 400m. A factor of 95% was applied for moose population estimates. We calculated 
the width of the 90% confidence interval by multiplying the t statistic for the left -tailed inverse of the Student’s t-
distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq root 
variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number of possible transects 
given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.  Due to the variation in transect lengths, 
population estimates were determined by Jolly’s (1969) method for sampling unequal sized units without 
replacement (Krebs 2014). 
 
Because of the timing of this survey some antler drop is expected to have happened, resulting in a male-skewed 
unclassified portion of the population, in particular for mule and white-tailed deer.  
Results 
Out of 144 possible transects, a total of 36 transects were surveyed for a total effort of 689 km2. Non-ungulate 
species observed during the survey included coyotes, porcupines, red fox, and snowy owls.  
There were 5 19 white-tailed deer observed within 107 groups. Of the 5 19 white-tailed deer observ ed:  
 
 39 (8%) were bucks 
 239 (46%) were does 
 140 (27%) were fawns 
 101 (19%) were not classified 
 
Of the 39 bucks identified, 7  (18%) were classified as small, 13  (33%) medium, 4 (10%) large, and 1 5 (38%) 
were unclassified. The buck: doe ratio was 0.16 and the fawn: doe ratio was 0.59 (Table 1). The average white-
tailed deer density was estimated at 0.88  individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 2402 
individuals (Table 1). This corresponds to a white -tailed deer population split estimate of 224 bucks, 1373 does 
and 804 fawns. 
 
There were 1216 mule deer observed within 202 groups. Of the 1216 mule deer identified:  
 
 250 (21%) were bucks 
 481 (40%) were does 
 331 (27%) were fawns 
 154 (13%) were not classified 
 
Of the 250 bucks observed, 54 (22%) were classified as small, 48 (19%) medium, 23 (9%) large and 125 (50%) 
were not classified. The buck: doe ratio was 0.52 and the fawn: doe ratio was 0.69 (Table 2).  The average mule 
deer density was estimated at 2.06 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 5628 individuals 
(Table 2). This corresponds to a mule deer population split estimate of 1325 bucks, 2549 does and 1754 fawns.  
 
There were 240 moose observed within 140 groups. Of the 240 moose identified:

 64 (27%) were bulls 
 91 (38%) were cows 
 75 (31%) were calves 
 10 (4%) were not classified 
The bull:cow ratio was 0.70 and the calf:cow ratio was 0.82 (Table 3).  The average moose density was estimated 
at 0.37 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 997 (Table 3) and corresponds to moose 
population split estimate of 277 bulls, 394 cows and 325 calves.  
Lastly, there were 41 elk (both on and off transect) observed within 10 groups. Of the 41 elk identified:  
 31 (76%) were bulls  
 7 (17%) were cows 
 3 (7%) were calves 
 0 (0%) were not classified
